title: Com Dev Ltd. (Mar 1999 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Ruling
subject: Aerospace and telecommunications company SR&ED appeal regarding eligible expenditures and proxy overhead calculations.
outcome: Appeal allowed in part; court clarified rules for allocating overhead and qualifying SR&ED project expenditures.
summary: In Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 775), the Tax Court of Canada ruled in 1999 that a CCPC's $28,350,000 in firm fixed-price subcontract payments from Spar were not SR&ED "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Payments from a prime contractor for hardware, not research, did not reduce its qualified expenditures or ITCs.
metaDescription: Read the March 1999 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Com Dev Ltd. concerning Canadian SR&ED tax credits and R&D expenditures.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Overview of the Taxpayer's Claim and Commercial Context

In Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (Docket 96-4343-IT-G, 99 DTC 775), the Tax Court of Canada adjudicated a landmark dispute concerning whether payments received by a specialized aerospace subcontractor under a firm fixed-price supply agreement constituted "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the Canadian Income Tax Act (the "Act"), which would otherwise eliminate the taxpayer's entitlement to Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs"). The Appellant, Com Dev Ltd. ("Com Dev"), was at all material times a Canadian-controlled private corporation ("CCPC") incorporated under the laws of Canada and headquartered in Cambridge, Ontario, carrying on an active business designing and manufacturing advanced subsystems and components for telecommunications and earth-observation spacecraft.

The commercial genesis of the appeal traced to January 26, 1990, when the Government of Canada (Her Majesty The Queen in Right of Canada) awarded a prime contract to Spar Aerospace Limited ("Spar") to act as general contractor for the design, construction, and integration of the "Radarsat" (Radarsat I) environmental monitoring satellite, scheduled for orbital launch in 1994. To execute the prime contract, Spar issued a Request for Proposal ("RFP") to various aerospace subcontractors for the design and manufacture of four critical spacecraft payload elements: the calibration system, the receiver system, the low power transmitter, and the phase shifters (collectively defined as the "Components"). Having established a substantial portfolio of pre-existing internal spacecraft technology—referred to in the aerospace sector as "heritage technology"—Com Dev was selected by Spar in 1989 under a letter of intent, which was subsequently formalized in a bilateral subcontract dated July 6, 1990 (the "Spar-Com Dev Contract") and amended six times in writing.

Executing the Spar-Com Dev Contract required Com Dev to undertake extensive internal engineering and experimental development to adapt its existing heritage technology to unprecedented performance specifications, evolving subsystem interfaces, and rigorous space-qualification standards. Com Dev completed delivery of the final flight-qualified Components to Spar in September 1994. Over the lifecycle of the subcontract, Com Dev received aggregate milestone remittances of $28,350,000 from Spar (the "Spar Payments"). However, because the Spar-Com Dev Contract was structured strictly on a firm fixed-price basis with stringent performance guarantees, Com Dev absorbed substantial uncompensated engineering cost overruns, ultimately suffering a net financial loss of $4,283,000 on the performance of the subcontract. For its 1989, 1990, 1991, and 1992 taxation years, Com Dev claimed SR&ED ITCs under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act on expenditures that the parties agreed qualified as SR&ED within the meaning of section 37 of the Act.
1.2 The Tax Authority's Challenge

By concurrent Notices of Reassessment dated December 16, 1994, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") reassessed Com Dev for the 1989, 1990, 1991, and 1992 taxation years. Remarkably, the Minister did not challenge the scientific or technological eligibility of Com Dev's activities; via a Partial Agreed Statement of Facts filed at the commencement of trial, both the Appellant and the Crown stipulated that Com Dev had incurred valid SR&ED expenditures within the meaning of section 37 of the Act and that those outlays constituted "qualified expenditures" within the base definition of subsection 127(9).

Instead, the Minister denied the ITCs claimed by Com Dev by invoking the statutory "contract payment" reduction rules under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 127(11.1)(c) of the Act. The Crown asserted that because the Radarsat program was ultimately funded by the federal government and because the Spar-Com Dev Contract contained a mandatory federal flow-down clause (Clause 12.3) purporting to vest all technical information and inventions in Her Majesty, Com Dev was functioning as a subcontractor performing SR&ED for or on behalf of the Canadian government. Consequently, the Minister characterized the entire $28,350,000 in Spar Payments as "contract payments" under paragraph (b) of the definition in subsection 127(9), and reduced Com Dev's qualified expenditures by the aggregate amount of the Spar Payments, which had the effect of reducing the ITCs claimed by Com Dev.
1.3 Governing Statutory Framework in Canada

As articulated by Judge Peter Dean Hamlyn of the Tax Court of Canada (citing Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724 (T.C.C.)), Parliament designed the statutory architecture of the Canadian SR&ED program to stimulate domestic technological innovation through a twofold fiscal incentive. First, under section 37 of the Act, qualifying SR&ED expenditures receive preferential income tax treatment, permitting taxpayers either to deduct such expenditures entirely in the taxation year incurred or to carry them forward indefinitely in a cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool for deduction in subsequent years. Second, subsection 127(5) of the Act permits a taxpayer to deduct an Investment Tax Credit from Part I tax otherwise payable (or, in the case of qualifying CCPCs, to receive a refundable credit), calculated as a statutory percentage of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" incurred in the year.

To prevent double-dipping—whereby a taxpayer claims ITCs on expenditures for which it has already been reimbursed or funded by another party—the Act mandated, through paragraph 127(11.1)(c) as it applied to the years under appeal, that "qualified expenditures" (and, under modern legislative numbering in subsections 127(18) and 127(19), the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool) be reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or "contract payments" that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. For amounts that became payable on or before December 20, 1991 (prior to the 1994 legislative amendments governing post-December 20, 1991 transactions), subsection 127(9) of the Act defined a "contract payment" across three distinct categories. Under paragraph (a), a contract payment encompassed an amount payable by a person resident in Canada for scientific research and experimental development related to the business of that person. Under paragraph (b), a contract payment encompassed an amount, other than a prescribed amount, payable by a Canadian government, municipality, or other Canadian public authority, or by a person exempt from tax under Part I by virtue of section 149, for scientific research and experimental development to be performed for it or on its behalf. Under paragraph (c), the definition captured an amount payable by a person not resident in Canada if that person was entitled to a deduction under clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(D) in respect of the amount, a provision that both parties stipulated in the Partial Agreed Statement of Facts had no application to the appeal.

While the definition was amended in 1994 for amounts that became payable after December 20, 1991 (a change to paragraph (b) that Judge Hamlyn found to be minimal and not to affect the determination in the case), and later amendments restructured paragraph (a) to reference amounts paid or payable by a "taxable supplier" for SR&ED performed "for, or on behalf of" a payer entitled to a deduction under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1) and added the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(25) ("deemed contract payment"), which applies where one of the main purposes of an arrangement with an arm's-length person is to cause an amount not to be a contract payment by having the performer paid by a person that is not a taxable supplier, the core statutory requirement of paragraph (b)—now shared by the current version of paragraph (a)—remains: the payment must be made for SR&ED to be performed for, or on behalf of, the payer. In Canadian tax administration, the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA") continues to list Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 775) alongside the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in The Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 DTC 6527) among the jurisprudence referenced in its official Assistance and Contract Payments Policy; that policy treats the distinction between a contract for services and a contract for the sale of goods as only one non-conclusive criterion (noting that a contract for the sale of a good does not necessarily mean that the SR&ED was not performed on behalf of the payer), while CCLC Technologies is cited in the policy for the test distinguishing government assistance from ordinary commercial payments.
1.4 The Tax Court of Canada's Final Holding

In a judgment signed on March 5, 1999 (released March 9, 1999), Judge Hamlyn allowed Com Dev's appeals in full for the 1989, 1990, 1991, and 1992 taxation years with costs. The Court applied the two-pronged legal test arising from the wording of paragraph (b) of the definition of "contract payment" in subsection 127(9), holding that for an amount to reduce a claimant's qualified expenditures under that provision, the Crown must establish both that the amount was payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or section 149 tax-exempt entity, and that the amount was payable specifically for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf.

The Tax Court ruled that the Minister failed on both prongs. First, applying the plain and ordinary meaning of the words of the definition, and declining to read into paragraph (b) the expansive "in respect of" language of paragraph 127(11.1)(c) that the Respondent urged be given its widest scope (citing Nowegijick v. The Queen ([1983] 1 S.C.R. 29)), the Court held that the $28,350,000 was payable by Spar—an arm's-length private commercial corporation—and not by the Government of Canada. No direct contractual relationship existed between Her Majesty and Com Dev, and there was no evidence that Spar acted merely as Her Majesty's agent. Second, examining the commercial substance of the transaction and looking beyond the contract to the collateral evidence because of potentially conflicting intellectual property clauses in the subcontract, the Court held that Spar contracted to purchase physical, flight-qualified hardware components at a firm fixed price, rather than SR&ED services or research results. Because Com Dev bore the entirety of the financial risk, retained ownership of its pre-existing heritage technology, and merely rearranged its proprietary know-how to deliver physical goods, the Spar Payments were commercial proceeds from the sale of goods rather than "contract payments" under subsection 127(9).
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

Although Com Dev ultimately prevailed before the Tax Court of Canada, the dispute exposes severe contractual, documentary, and evidentiary vulnerabilities that routinely trigger CRA audit denials, alongside the legal errors committed by the Crown in evaluating multi-tier procurement arrangements. An anatomical examination of the trial record reveals four primary clusters of legal and evidentiary failure that led to more than four years of litigation between the December 16, 1994 reassessments and the March 1999 judgment.
2.1 Contractual Drafting Contradictions: The Collision of Crown Boilerplate (Clause 12.3) and Proprietary Carve-Outs (Clause 12.7)

The single greatest catalyst for the Minister's reassessment was a glaring internal contradiction within the intellectual property provisions of the Spar-Com Dev Contract. Under its prime contract with the Government of Canada, Spar was contractually obligated by the Crown to flow down a standard federal procurement clause—designated as Clause 12.3—into all subcontracts. Clause 12.3 stipulated verbatim that all technical information and inventions conceived or developed or first actually reduced to practice in performing the work under the contract would become the property of Her Majesty, and that the contractor would have no rights therein except as provided by Her Majesty. Furthermore, Clause 12.3 prohibited Com Dev, without the express written permission of Her Majesty, from divulging or using such technical information and inventions other than in performing the Work under the contract, and from selling articles embodying them other than to Spar under the contract. Standing alone, Clause 12.3 created an overwhelming prima facie presumption for tax auditors that the federal government was funding and acquiring the beneficial ownership of all SR&ED conducted by Com Dev.

Rather than excising or redrafting Clause 12.3, Spar included it in the subcontract but also included—on the recommendation of Spar's own Radarsat hardware programmer, Mr. Bill Chisholm, and with Spar's full approval—a diminution modification provision, Clause 12.7, which incorporated by reference an external letter dated April 19, 1990 from John Berry (Contract Administrator at Com Dev) to Terry Littlewood (Subcontracts Manager at Spar). That letter certified that all equipment, associated technical information, and technical documentation to be generated and delivered under the subcontract would utilize computer software, processes, methods, techniques, and know-how in existence or residence with Com Dev prior to the effective date of the contract, and declared that the intellectual property in such pre-existing software, processes, methods, techniques, and know-how was proprietary to Com Dev and could solely be used for the purposes of the Radarsat programme.

Because the contract simultaneously purported to vest all arising inventions in Her Majesty (Clause 12.3) while certifying that the entire technological foundation of the deliverables remained the exclusive property of Com Dev (Clause 12.7), the written agreement contained potentially conflicting clauses that did not allow it simply to speak for itself. At trial, the Respondent pleaded that the contract spoke for itself, relying on the explicit Crown vesting language of Clause 12.3 to characterize the arrangement as one under which the intellectual property arising from the work was to be transferred to the Government of Canada. Because the intellectual property articles were not harmonized at inception, Judge Hamlyn held that he was not bound by the parol evidence rule and could look beyond the contract to the collateral evidence—including the testimony of Ms. Anita Carol Davis, Mr. Bill Chisholm, Dr. Bertram Blevis, and Mr. David Belbeck and the parties' conduct under the contract—to determine the intention of the contracting parties.
2.2 Statement of Work and Deliverable Characterization: Distinguishing Flight-Qualification Documentation from SR&ED Results

A second major vulnerability arose from the technical terminology deployed in the subcontract's scope of work and the volume of technical data delivered to Spar. The Respondent argued that under the express terms of the contract, Com Dev became a subcontractor of Spar for the research, design, development, analysis, testing, verification, and delivery of subsystems to be integrated into Radarsat, that Com Dev was required to perform SR&ED in order to do so, and that the intention was to transfer to the Government of Canada the intellectual property arising from the entire performance of the contract; the evidence also showed that the information accompanying the Components provided a historical outline tracking the product from design to flight model.

This dispute highlights a perennial technical-legal pitfall in advanced manufacturing and aerospace contracts: the conflation of quality assurance and interface verification documentation with SR&ED research deliverables. In space-qualification procurement, a prime contractor cannot integrate a complex payload subsystem into a satellite bus without receiving comprehensive telemetry interfaces, thermal and structural test logs, reliability verifications, and operational tracking manuals. Com Dev argued that the Minister's position treated the delivery of this accompanying Component Information—which is typically required by a purchaser of components in the aerospace industry—as the delivery of SR&ED. To overcome this characterization at trial, Com Dev adduced testimony from its Vice President (Ms. Davis) that the information transferred was to ensure the functionality and reliability of the Components, fact testimony from Spar's hardware programmer (Mr. Chisholm) that at no time did Com Dev deliver research and development results to Spar nor were any expected, and expert testimony (Dr. Bertram Blevis) that the Components and accompanying documentation were consistent in the industry with a contract for the sale of a product; Com Dev further submitted that the Component Information would not be sufficient for Spar or anyone retained by Spar to duplicate the Components.
2.3 Collateral Documentary Vulnerabilities: Conference Acknowledgments, Document Annotations, and Internal Memoranda

At trial, in support of the argument that the intellectual property belonged to Her Majesty, the Respondent relied on three items of collateral documentation that threatened to derail the Appellant's legal position. First, the Respondent produced an annotation appearing on some technical documents (Exhibit A-1, tabs 28 to 34). Second, the Respondent relied on an acknowledgement at the end of a paper presented by Com Dev to a space conference (Exhibit A-1 Supplemental, tab 9, page 130). Third, the Respondent produced an internal correspondence from Com Dev warning Com Dev employees about using information that rightfully belongs to other companies in documents submitted to Spar (Exhibit A-1, tab 37).

In many SR&ED disputes before the Tax Court of Canada, contemporaneous internal memos and public statements acknowledging government sponsorship are treated as damaging admissions against interest. In Com Dev, Judge Hamlyn found that this evidence did not change the Court's review of the evidence in relation to the contractual relationship and the intention of the parties—evidence that included the firm fixed-price risk structure, the $4,283,000 financial loss, and Spar's post-contract proposal to buy the technology from Com Dev for Radarsat II. Nevertheless, these collateral documents gave the Respondent material with which to contend that the intellectual property in question belonged to Her Majesty.
2.4 The Minister's Analytical and Evidentiary Deficiencies: Privity, Agency, Risk Allocation, and the "Sale of Goods" Doctrine

While Com Dev's contractual ambiguities and collateral documentation triggered the reassessment, the ultimate failure in the courtroom belonged to the Minister of National Revenue. The Crown's legal theory suffered from four fatal analytical and evidentiary defects regarding privity, economic risk allocation, buyer monitoring, and post-contract conduct.

First, the Minister disregarded fundamental principles of contractual privity and agency law. Under paragraph (b) of subsection 127(9), an amount must be "payable by" a Canadian government or public authority. The Minister attempted to collapse a two-tier contractual chain (Crown-to-Spar and Spar-to-Com Dev) into a single direct funding conduit, submitting that the $28,350,000 was paid by the Government of Canada because Spar was merely a general contractor through which all payments flowed, the project was fully funded by the Government of Canada, and Her Majesty was mentioned in numerous provisions of the Spar-Com Dev Contract. The Crown failed to adduce any evidence establishing a principal-agent relationship between Her Majesty and Spar. On the contrary, the evidence proved that Spar contracted with Com Dev on its own commercial account at arm's length, and when Com Dev suffered a $4,283,000 loss, it was unable to claim compensation from the Government of Canada because there was no contractual relationship between Com Dev and the Government of Canada; any request for compensation had to be presented to Spar, which had the option of submitting it to the Government of Canada and chose not to do so.

Second, the Minister failed to evaluate the economic risk allocation distinguishing a fixed-price commercial supply contract from a cost-plus research retainer. As testified by Ms. Davis, a cost contract is usually the vehicle applied in a research and development retainer, and a cost-plus structure is one in which risk is borne by the contractor rather than the subcontractor, payments are not based on results, and profits are protected; Dr. Blevis likewise distinguished within the industry between contracts for the sale of goods and contracts for research and development, reviewing distinguishing features such as firm fixed pricing, payment schedules, performance guarantees, and technology protection. Conversely, the Spar-Com Dev Contract was a firm fixed-price contract with milestone payments strictly contingent upon the physical achievement of production results and backed by rigid performance guarantees. By bearing 100% of the financial risk of technological uncertainty—culminating in a $4,283,000 loss—Com Dev performed the SR&ED on its own behalf to fulfill a commercial obligation to deliver hardware.

Third, the Crown erroneously conflated buyer risk-phasing with the direction of SR&ED. The Respondent placed emphasis on the references to Her Majesty throughout the Spar-Com Dev Contract, and the evidence showed that the work was phased by Spar to Com Dev to meet Her Majesty's requirements and that Her Majesty had the right to monitor the progress of the Components. The Court held that the mention of Her Majesty did not change the commercial reality of the relationship, accepting evidence that such monitoring arrangements are common in the aerospace industry when the ultimate success of the overall project depends in part on products produced by subcontractors, and that the phasing served to protect the integrity of the project against the risk of failure; the right to monitor did not change the fact that there was no direct contractual relationship between Com Dev and Her Majesty, and there was no evidence that Spar acted merely as Her Majesty's agent.

Fourth, the Minister was wholly unable to rebut the probative force of the parties' post-contract commercial conduct regarding the Radarsat II program. The Crown's assertion that Clause 12.3 transferred all arising intellectual property and SR&ED results to the Government of Canada was fatally undermined by Mr. Belbeck's uncontroverted documentary evidence showing that, following the expiration of the Radarsat I subcontract, Spar approached Com Dev with a commercial proposal to buy the underlying technology from Com Dev for the subsequent Radarsat II program to perform the exact same subsystem functions. As Judge Hamlyn observed, the actions of the parties under the contract supported their stated intention: Spar showed no interest in the technology and later offered to buy it from Com Dev for the Radarsat II project, and there was no evidence that Her Majesty asserted or attempted to obtain any of the intellectual property that the Respondent maintained was the property of Her Majesty; had Spar or the Crown already acquired the SR&ED results under Clause 12.3, Spar would have had no reason to offer to purchase that technology.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement adjudicated in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen against the underlying contractual/documentary vulnerability (and the Minister's resulting legal challenge), the taxpayer's evidentiary rebuttal, and the governing standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Holding

cells: Base SR&ED Eligibility & Qualified Expenditures (Income Tax Act, s. 37(1) & s. 127(9))

Not disputed at trial; the Respondent admitted that the amounts were "qualified expenditures" that would qualify for the ITC if subsection 127(9) were read without reference to paragraph 127(11.1)(c).
Partial Agreed Statement of Facts filed at trial stipulating that expenditures qualified as SR&ED under s. 37 and met the base definition of "qualified expenditures" under s. 127(9).

Where the Crown concedes technical eligibility under s. 37, the inquiry shifts exclusively to whether statutory reductions—here, solely "contract payments" under paragraph (b) of the definition in s. 127(9), applied through paragraph 127(11.1)(c)—erode the qualified expenditures.
Prong 1 of Paragraph 127(9)(b): "Payable by a Canadian Government..." (Direct Liability & Privity of Contract)

Ultimate project funding for Radarsat originated from the Government of Canada; prime contract terms and references to Her Majesty were flowed down into the Spar-Com Dev Contract. The Minister argued the $28.35M was indirectly paid by the Crown.

Testimony of CFO (D. Belbeck), VP (A. Davis), and Spar's Radarsat hardware programmer (B. Chisholm) proving no privity of contract existed between Com Dev and the Crown; Com Dev could not claim against the Crown for its $4,283,000 loss.

Plain and Ordinary Meaning Standard: The plain and ordinary meaning of "contract payment" applies, and the expansive "in respect of" language of paragraph 127(11.1)(c) (for which the Respondent cited Nowegijick) is not read into paragraph (b); the payments arose from the rights and obligations under the Spar-Com Dev Contract, were paid by Spar rather than Her Majesty, and there was no direct contractual relationship with, and no evidence of agency for, the Crown. Ultimate economic funding source does not override corporate and contractual privity.
Absence of Principal-Agent Relationship (Prime Contractor vs. Crown Agent)

Spar phased the subcontract and enforced government monitoring rights and cost controls to satisfy Her Majesty's prime contract requirements. The Crown argued Spar acted as a conduit/agent for Her Majesty.

Testimony of B. Chisholm and expert Dr. B. Blevis proving Spar contracted on its own commercial account at arm's length; monitoring arrangements are common in the aerospace industry, and phasing protected the integrity of the project against the risk of failure.

Contractual flow-down of buyer inspection, monitoring, and milestone phasing in a complex supply chain represents commercial risk management and does not constitute legal agency on behalf of the Crown.
Prong 2 of Paragraph 127(9)(b): "For SR&ED to be Performed For It or On Its Behalf" (Sale of Goods vs. R&D Service Contract)

Subcontract SOW required Com Dev to "research, design, develop, analyze, test, verify, and deliver" subsystems. The Minister argued the contract was inherently a subcontract for the performance of SR&ED.

Testimony of A. Davis and expert Dr. B. Blevis establishing industry commercial norms (firm fixed-price structure, milestone payments tied to production results, performance guarantees), and testimony of CFO D. Belbeck that Com Dev absorbed a $4.283M loss.

Commercial Substance & Risk Allocation Test: On the evidence in this case, a firm fixed-price contract for the purchase of physical components, with milestone payments linked to production results and risk at all times in the hands of the vendor—contrasted with a cost-plus R&D retainer—did not include the purchase of SR&ED (the CRA notes that the sale-of-goods characterization is not, by itself, conclusive).
Intellectual Property Ownership & Contractual Ambiguity (Clause 12.3 vs. Clause 12.7 & April 19, 1990 Letter)

Clause 12.3 (Crown boilerplate) explicitly vested all Technical Information and Inventions conceived or reduced to practice under the contract in Her Majesty. The Minister relied on Clause 12.3 to prove Crown acquisition of SR&ED.

Introduction of Clause 12.7 and the April 19, 1990 Letter modifying Clause 12.3 and certifying all deliverables relied on pre-existing proprietary "heritage technology" retained by Com Dev; corroborated by Spar's subsequent offer to buy the IP for Radarsat II.

Parol Evidence & Post-Contract Conduct Standard: Because Clause 12.3 was diminished by Clause 12.7 (at a minimum severely restricting Her Majesty's proprietary interest), the potentially conflicting clauses did not allow the contract simply to speak for itself; the Court was not bound by the parol evidence rule and examined collateral evidence and the parties' conduct (such as the post-contract offer to purchase the technology), finding that Com Dev retained the rights to its pre-existing technology.
Nature of Technical Documentation Deliverables (Operational Verification vs. SR&ED Know-How)

Com Dev delivered extensive technical tracking and test documentation alongside the hardware, which contained government contract annotations. The Minister argued this constituted delivery of SR&ED information.

Testimony of A. Davis (information ensured functionality and reliability and tracked the product from design to flight model), B. Chisholm (no R&D results delivered or expected), and Dr. B. Blevis (documentation consistent with a sale of product), together with Com Dev's submission that the information was insufficient to allow Spar or anyone retained by Spar to duplicate the Components.

Standard quality assurance, interface, and operational tracking documentation accompanying complex hardware does not equate to the transfer of underlying SR&ED methodology or proprietary design know-how.
Collateral Documentary Admissions (Conference Papers & Internal Memos)

An annotation on some technical documents, an acknowledgement at the end of a paper Com Dev presented to a space conference, and an internal Com Dev correspondence warning employees about using information belonging to other companies in documents submitted to Spar. The Minister cited these as admissions of Crown-funded SR&ED.
Witness testimony, the contract terms, and the parties' conduct establishing the fixed-price commercial relationship and the intention of the parties, against which the Court weighed these documents.
The Court found that this collateral evidence did not change its review of the evidence in relation to the contractual relationship and the intention of the parties.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen into contemporary Canadian tax practice, tax counsel and technical advisors must account for both the enduring "sale of goods versus performance of SR&ED" doctrine established by Judge Hamlyn and the modern statutory architecture of the Income Tax Act—specifically paragraph 127(9)(a) ("taxable supplier" rules), paragraph 127(9)(b) (government and public authority payments), and subsection 127(25) (the "deemed contract payment" anti-avoidance rule). While subsection 127(25) deems an amount to be a contract payment where one of the main purposes of an arrangement with an arm's-length person is to cause the amount not to be a contract payment—by having the amount paid to a taxable supplier while the performer is paid by a person that is not a taxable supplier—subsection 127(25) and subsection 127(9) only apply if the payment received by the performer is in fact "in respect of" or "for" SR&ED performed for or on behalf of the payer. Thus, Judge Hamlyn's second prong—whether the amount was payable for SR&ED to be performed for or on behalf of the payer, which in Com Dev turned on evidence that the subcontract was a firm fixed-price contract for the purchase of physical components incorporating the vendor's retained heritage intellectual property, with risk at all times in the vendor's hands—remains a central line of defence for Canadian innovators, although the CRA cautions that no single criterion is conclusive and that a contract for the sale of a good does not necessarily mean that the SR&ED was not performed on behalf of the payer.

The following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how Canadian corporate taxpayers facing the exact legal and documentary pitfalls identified in Com Dev can proactively restructure their project governance, contractual terms, technical deliverables, and experimentation tracking to withstand CRA audit scrutiny and preserve full SR&ED ITC eligibility.
4.1 Case Study 1: Aerospace & Defence Subcontracting (Quantum-Secured Satellite Optical Transceiver)
Scenario & Impending Legal Pitfalls

AetherPhotonics Inc. ("Aether"), a CCPC based in Ottawa, Ontario, specializes in free-space optical communication subsystems. CanSpace Prime Corp. ("CanSpace"), a major Canadian aerospace prime contractor, has been awarded a $180 million prime contract by the Department of National Defence ("DND") and the Canadian Space Agency ("CSA") to build a low-earth-orbit ("LEO") tactical communications satellite constellation. CanSpace selects Aether as a Tier-1 subcontractor under a $15 million arrangement to supply four flight-qualified Quantum-Secured Optical Transceiver ("QSOT") units.

To meet CanSpace's unprecedented pointing-accuracy and radiation-hardening specifications, Aether must invest $6.5 million in internal SR&ED to adapt its pre-existing terrestrial laser-communication architecture ("Heritage Optical Platform"). However, Aether's draft subcontract contains four critical vulnerabilities mirroring the exact audit triggers in Com Dev. First, CanSpace has pasted verbatim Public Services and Procurement Canada ("PSPC") Standard Acquisition Clauses vesting all "Foreground Information" (inventions and technical data conceived or first reduced to practice under the contract) in His Majesty The King in Right of Canada, analogous to Clause 12.3 in Com Dev. Second, the Statement of Work ("SOW") is titled "Subcontract for the Research, Design, Prototyping, Verification, and Delivery of QSOT Subsystems," with milestone payments tied to Preliminary Design Review ("PDR"), Critical Design Review ("CDR"), Engineering Qualification Model ("EQM") test reports, and Flight Model ("FM") delivery. Third, because federal funds flow from DND and CSA through CanSpace (a taxable Canadian corporation) to Aether, a CRA auditor can attack the $15 million receipts as a "contract payment" from a taxable supplier under paragraph 127(9)(a), and may also scrutinize the federal funding chain under paragraph 127(9)(b) and the deemed contract payment rule in subsection 127(25) (although Com Dev held that ultimate government funding through an arm's-length prime contractor does not, by itself, make an amount payable by a government), potentially wiping out Aether's $6.5 million qualified expenditure pool. Fourth, Aether's optical physicists plan to present their radiation-hardening experimental findings at an upcoming IEEE conference with a slide acknowledging DND and CSA funding, while Aether's CAD templates automatically stamp "Property of His Majesty / DND LEO Program" on all engineering schematics.
Step 1: Project Governance & Risk Architecture Restructuring

Aether must first establish an airtight administrative and financial boundary separating its commercial hardware supply obligation to CanSpace from its internal, self-directed SR&ED program. To accomplish this, Aether's Board of Directors and Vice President of Engineering must formally charter an internal SR&ED project (Project Code SRED-OPT-400: Sub-Microradian Cryogenic Beam Steering & III-V Semiconductor Radiation Tolerance) prior to or independently of the commercial manufacturing order (Commercial Job Code MFG-CANSPACE-01). The internal corporate charter must explicitly document that Aether is undertaking the SR&ED on its own behalf to upgrade its proprietary Heritage Optical Platform for broad commercial exploitation across global commercial satellite constellations, rather than exclusively for CanSpace.

Concurrently, corporate governance minutes and financial control policies must explicitly record that Aether assumes 100% of the financial risk of cost overruns, yield failures, and rework under the CanSpace supply contract. No cost-plus change orders, research labour rate schedules, or time-and-materials billing mechanisms may be permitted in the commercial relationship with CanSpace, thereby mirroring the exact economic risk allocation that persuaded Judge Hamlyn in Com Dev.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring & Intellectual Property Harmonization

To avoid the potential conflict between Clause 12.3 and Clause 12.7 that required the Court in Com Dev to look beyond the contract to collateral evidence at trial, Aether's tax and commercial counsel must redraft the subcontract prior to execution. Rather than leaving the PSPC Foreground IP vesting clause untouched and appending a contradictory side letter, Aether must explicitly subordinate any mandatory government flow-down schedule within the Master Terms and Conditions (Article 1.2 - Order of Precedence), stipulating that the Specific Commercial Terms override all annexed government flow-down appendices in the event of conflict.

Within those Specific Commercial Terms, counsel must draft a comprehensive Intellectual Property Article certifying three foundational legal facts: first, that Aether was selected as a vendor due to its pre-existing ownership of the Heritage Optical Platform; second, that all core optical designs, beam-steering algorithms, semiconductor packaging processes, and fabrication know-how—including all internal modifications, rearrangements, and adaptations thereof required to meet the environmental specifications of the QSOT units—constitute Aether's exclusive proprietary property; and third, that neither CanSpace nor His Majesty acquires any ownership interest in Aether's underlying technology, processes, or SR&ED results, receiving only a non-exclusive license to operate the delivered physical QSOT hardware units aboard the LEO constellation.

Furthermore, the agreement must be retitled "Firm Fixed-Price Commercial Supply Agreement for Flight-Qualified QSOT Hardware Units," and the Statement of Work must be purged of any references to Aether being hired to "perform research," "conduct experimental development," or "deliver R&D studies". The PDR and CDR milestones must be contractually defined strictly as Commercial Risk-Mitigation and Interface Verification Gates required to confirm that the physical goods being manufactured will mechanically, thermally, and electrically mate with CanSpace's satellite bus, explicitly stating that milestone payments represent partial prepayments of the fixed purchase price for physical goods under provincial sale of goods legislation. Finally, the contract must include a Future Generation Commercial Exploitation Clause confirming that Aether retains the unrestricted right to sell optical transceivers embodying the adapted technology to third-party commercial customers, and that any subsequent generation of satellites (such as LEO Constellation Phase II) will require CanSpace to purchase additional physical units or negotiate a separate commercial technology license from Aether—codifying on the face of the agreement the evidentiary factor (the Radarsat II purchase proposal) that the Court relied upon as supporting the parties' stated intention in Com Dev.
Step 3: Technical Documentation & Deliverable Segregation

Aether must erect a strict operational firewall between the Interface and Qualification Data Package ("IQDP") delivered to CanSpace and the Internal SR&ED Design and Experimentation Repository retained at Aether's facility. The IQDP delivered at PDR, CDR, and FM acceptance must be restricted strictly to "black-box" form, fit, and function specifications: external mechanical dimensions, pin-out telemetry protocols, power consumption curves, and pass/fail environmental vibration and thermal-vacuum certification logs. Under no circumstances may Aether deliver source code, internal optical bench failure analyses, iterative hypothesis testing logs, or semiconductor doping recipes that would enable CanSpace, DND, or a third-party manufacturer to duplicate the QSOT units.

To eliminate the documentary blemishes cited by the Crown in Com Dev, Aether must replace all CAD and document headers stating "Property of His Majesty" with a standardized proprietary legend: "PROPRIETARY & CONFIDENTIAL PROPERTY OF AETHERPHOTONICS INC. – Furnished strictly for form, fit, and function integration of commercial hardware under Supply Contract #MFG-CANSPACE-01. Contains no transferable design or manufacturing rights". Simultaneously, Aether must enforce a mandatory Legal and Tax Pre-Clearance Policy for all academic and conference papers, prohibiting engineers from stating that DND, CSA, or CanSpace "funded" or "sponsored" the R&D; approved acknowledgments may state only that the commercial hardware specifications were informed by mission parameters of the Canadian LEO program.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation & Financial Tracking

To satisfy section 37 and subsection 127(9) during a CRA technical and financial review, Aether must align its internal tracking with the established Canadian jurisprudence for SR&ED eligibility while proving strict cost segregation. Aether's engineering team must maintain contemporaneous laboratory notebooks and digital engineering tickets under Project Code SRED-OPT-400 documenting the specific technological uncertainties—specifically, why standard terrestrial Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers suffer catastrophic photodarkening under LEO proton flux, and why existing piezo-actuators fail to maintain sub-microradian lock under satellite micro-vibrations—and logging each sequential hypothesis, experimental simulation, breadboard iteration, and test failure separately from routine commercial assembly of the final flight units.

In the financial general ledger, all SR&ED labour, non-commercial experimental breadboards, and materials consumed or transformed during the experimental phase must be tracked in dedicated accounts mapped to SRED-OPT-400. Commercial manufacturing of the final four flight units (once technological uncertainty is resolved) must be booked separately to Cost of Goods Sold ("COGS") under MFG-CANSPACE-01, ensuring that whether the commercial supply contract yields a profit or an uncompensated loss, Aether can demonstrate both the exact quantum of section 37 SR&ED expenditures and its autonomous assumption of commercial risk.
4.2 Case Study 2: Clean-Tech & Advanced Manufacturing (Hydrogen Fuel Cell Stack Subsystems for a Municipal Transit Consortium)
Scenario & Impending Legal Pitfalls

HydraCore Power Systems Ltd. ("HydraCore"), a CCPC based in Mississauga, Ontario, designs and manufactures proton-exchange membrane ("PEM") fuel cell stacks. A coalition of three major Canadian municipal transit authorities (each a "municipality or other Canadian public authority" under paragraph 127(9)(b) of the Act) awards a $90 million contract to TransitBus OEM Inc. ("TransitBus"), a taxable Canadian heavy-vehicle manufacturer, to supply 60 zero-emission hydrogen fuel cell articulated buses. TransitBus enters into an $8.4 million subcontract with HydraCore to supply 60 heavy-duty 150-kW PEM fuel cell power modules capable of operating reliably at ambient temperatures down to −40°C without external battery freeze-start heating.

While HydraCore possesses a proven 100-kW commercial fuel cell architecture ("Gen-3 PEM Core") operable to −15°C, achieving unassisted cold-start at −40°C at 150-kW power density presents fundamental electrochemical and fluid-dynamic uncertainties, specifically ice-lens formation delaminating the catalyst-coated membrane during sub-zero purge cycles. HydraCore incurs $3.2 million in qualifying SR&ED expenditures over two taxation years to overcome these uncertainties, ultimately absorbing a $950,000 commercial loss on the $8.4 million contract due to membrane scrap and iterative stack rebuilds.

However, HydraCore faces four severe audit exposures under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(25). First, TransitBus is a "taxable supplier" resident in Canada (triggering paragraph 127(9)(a) if the contract is characterized as SR&ED performed for or on behalf of TransitBus), while the underlying capital funding originates from Canadian municipalities (inviting scrutiny under paragraph 127(9)(b) and the subsection 127(25) deemed contract payment rule if characterized as SR&ED performed on behalf of the municipal authorities, notwithstanding Com Dev's holding that ultimate public funding through an arm's-length contractor does not by itself make an amount payable by a public authority). Second, HydraCore's sales team structured the $8.4 million contract price into two explicit invoice schedules: Schedule A ($2.4 million) billed as "Non-Recurring Engineering, Cold-Start R&D, and Prototype Validation Services," and Schedule B ($6.0 million) billed as "$100,000 per delivered 150-kW Fuel Cell Module (60 units)"—making Schedule A a smoking-gun admission of a $2.4 million "contract payment" for SR&ED. Third, the municipal transit consortium funded 50% of the procurement through a green-transit capital subsidy whose terms, flowed down into the TransitBus-HydraCore subcontract, state that all "Project Technical Developments and Environmental Test Data" may be freely shared by the municipalities with other transit agencies and third-party maintenance contractors across Canada. Fourth, HydraCore's CFO circulated an internal budget memo stating that TransitBus's $2.4 million NRE payment would cover 75% of HydraCore's −40°C R&D budget, the type of internal document that, like the internal correspondence relied on by the Crown in Com Dev, can be cited against the taxpayer at trial.
Step 1: Project Governance & Risk Architecture Restructuring

HydraCore must immediately eliminate the structural characterization that it is performing contracted R&D services for TransitBus or the municipalities, anchoring the transaction squarely within the commercial "sale of goods" framework of Com Dev. HydraCore's commercial governance committee must institute a strict policy prohibiting sales personnel from quoting or contracting separately for "Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE)" or "R&D Services" when the commercial substance of the arrangement is the supply of commercial hardware units. Instead, the entire $8.4 million consideration must be governed and priced as an integrated, firm fixed-price unit supply contract ($140,000 per commercial 150-kW module across 60 units), with tiered deposit and progress payments tied strictly to commercial production readiness and unit deliveries.

Furthermore, corporate governance records and risk committee minutes must emphasize that HydraCore provides binding commercial performance warranties—specifically, −40°C startup within 90 seconds and a 15,000-hour stack durability guarantee—backed by liquidated damages for late delivery or field failure. Formally documenting that HydraCore bears the full downside risk of the $950,000 cost overrun, with zero contractual recourse against TransitBus or the municipal consortium, establishes the exact economic risk profile relied upon by Judge Hamlyn in Com Dev.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring & Intellectual Property Harmonization

HydraCore's legal counsel must execute a comprehensive contractual restatement or written amendment prior to performing the work—analogous to the Clause 12.7 modification in Com Dev, but drafted to eliminate any residual ambiguity. First, counsel must abolish Schedule A ("NRE and Cold-Start R&D Services") in its entirety and structure the agreement exclusively as a Master Commercial Component Purchase Agreement for 60 physical 150-kW PEM fuel cell modules. Where upfront cash flow is commercially required prior to full assembly of the 60 units, the contract must characterize initial remittances strictly as Non-Refundable Commercial Tooling and Production Capacity Reservation Deposits credited against the per-unit purchase price of the physical goods upon delivery.

Second, to neutralize the municipal data-sharing flow-down clause, counsel must insert a definitive proprietary carve-out clause (analogous to Clause 12.7 and the April 19, 1990 letter in Com Dev, but elevated to an overriding primary representation) certifying that the 150-kW modules are built upon HydraCore's pre-existing proprietary Gen-3 PEM Core heritage technology. The clause must explicitly define the "Environmental Test Data" shareable with the municipalities as being restricted solely to external vehicle-level diagnostic fault codes, hydrogen fuel consumption rates, and routine preventative maintenance schedules such as air filter and coolant replacement intervals.

Third, the agreement must expressly reserve all electrochemical and stack intellectual property to HydraCore, stipulating that all internal membrane-electrode assembly ("MEA") formulations, bipolar plate micro-channel geometries, sub-zero purge algorithms, and experimental test data conceived, developed, or utilized by HydraCore remain the sole and exclusive intellectual property of HydraCore, and that neither TransitBus nor any municipal authority receives any right to access, disclose, or manufacture the internal stack components. The contract should further prohibit TransitBus and the municipalities from disassembling or reverse-engineering the sealed fuel cell stack enclosures.
Step 3: Technical Documentation & Deliverable Segregation

HydraCore must ensure that the technical packages transmitted to TransitBus and the municipal authorities cannot be mischaracterized by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor ("RTA") or Financial Reviewer as the delivery of SR&ED results. Deliverables provided to TransitBus and the municipal transit fleet engineers must consist solely of CAN-bus electronic control unit ("ECU") communication protocols, mechanical mounting drawings, safety interlock certifications, and external cold-chamber pass/fail verification certificates confirming that the completed commercial unit started at −40°C. All internal SR&ED documentation—including scanning electron microscopy ("SEM") analyses of ice-damaged catalyst layers, computational fluid dynamics ("CFD") models of two-phase water transport during sub-zero purge, and failed prototype stack teardowns—must be classified as Internal Trade Secrets and withheld entirely from TransitBus.

To remediate internal documentary vulnerabilities, HydraCore must establish a corporate tax communications protocol educating finance and engineering executives on the legal distinction between commercial product revenue and funded SR&ED. Rather than describing customer deposits in board minutes as "NRE funding covering our R&D budget," financial reports and board resolutions must accurately record that customer receipts represent deferred commercial revenue from the fixed-price sale of 60 physical fuel cell modules, while internal SR&ED expenditures under section 37 represent self-funded corporate investments in HydraCore's proprietary Gen-4 PEM technology platform.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation & Financial Tracking

To substantiate the $3.2 million SR&ED claim under section 37 while insulating it from any subsection 127(9) reduction, HydraCore must implement a bifurcated technical and accounting protocol. On the technical side, HydraCore must maintain a dedicated internal SR&ED project dossier (SRED-PEM-COLD-04) structured around the systematic investigation of technological uncertainty: documenting why existing Gen-3 PEM knowledge and publicly available electrochemistry literature cannot predict the coupled phase-change and membrane proton-conductivity behaviour when current density is ramped at −40°C without parasitic external heaters, and contemporaneously logging each experimental hypothesis (such as varying hydrophobic PTFE concentrations in the gas diffusion layer versus pulsed high-frequency AC impedance self-heating during purge), the exact experimental bench protocols executed on 5-cell short-stack test rigs, quantitative test results, and analytical conclusions demonstrating technological advancement.

On the accounting side, HydraCore must enforce a strict separation between experimental short-stacks and commercial production units. All time-sheet hours, experimental catalyst batches, and 5-cell test-rig materials consumed in resolving the cold-start uncertainty must be tracked exclusively within the SRED-PEM-COLD-04 cost centre. Once the final MEA formulation and purge algorithm are frozen and validated, all subsequent procurement of materials and assembly labour for the 60 commercial 150-kW units delivered to TransitBus must be charged exclusively to the commercial manufacturing job ledger (MFG-TRANSIT-60). By proving that the experimental short-stacks were scrapped or retained in HydraCore's laboratory and never delivered to TransitBus, and that TransitBus received only sealed, commercial production modules under a fixed-price contract of sale, HydraCore establishes an evidentiary record aligned with the factors relied upon by the Tax Court of Canada in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen.
